paper_title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) extend the reasoning that Large Language Models (LLMs) acquire from text to video, an input of rich, dynamic visual semantics (Bai et al., 2025b;a; Li et al., 2025; Clark et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026). Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains the established stage for adapting pretrained VideoLLM to downstream task (Bai et al., 2025b) and grounding that reasoning in the video. Even recent methods trained with reinforcement learning (RL) retain this stage as the basis of their improvement (Wang et al., 2025a;b). While SFT is thus core element in advancing VideoLLMs, it is prone to learning superficial correlations rather than reading the modality it is given. These correlations, which we call shortcuts (Geirhos et al., 2020; Dancette et al., 2021), are regularities of the training set that predict the label within the training distribution but may not hold outside it. Video QA is especially susceptible, as many questions can be answered from regularities in the text alone (Yang et al., 2025), and SFT readily comes to rely on them (Li et al., 2023; Chen & Li, 2026). Existing approaches counter shortcut by filtering it from the data (Chen et al., 2020; Shvetsova et al., 2025), penalizing it in the loss (Cadene et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019; Niu et al., 2021; Chen & Li, 2026), or adjusting the trained model or its decoding afterward (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Filtering has to define which regularity counts as the shortcut before it can act (Dancette et al., 2021), while the regularities fine-tuning will pick up are rarely known in advance, and the loss and the trained model constrain what the model outputs rather than the update through which the shortcut is written. remedy would instead have to act where the shortcut forms, which raises our central question: where does the shortcut form in the course of fine-tuning, and can fine-tuning be constrained there to suppress it? To address this question, we track how the reliance of VideoLLM on the text changes over SFT, both within the training distribution and under distribution shift. We fine-tune on filtered video QA data where the text alone gives the base model little ground for its answer. After training, the Corresponding authors.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: SFT builds shortcut, and VETO suppresses it. Accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B against its text-only accuracy, where rise indicates the shortcut. (a) Within the training distribution (SSv2) SFT and VETO reach similar gain in accuracy, but the shortcut grows much more under SFT. (b) Under the shift (Perception Test) VETO gains accuracy whereas SFT gains only the shortcut. VideoLLM answers far more questions from the text alone than the base model does, regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. Within the training distribution, this may seem to cost nothing, since full-input accuracy rises alongside it, as Fig. 1(a) shows. Under the shift, however, the gain of the fine-tuned model over the base model is limited, while its accuracy from the text alone still rises above the base model on every benchmark. In other words, the shortcut fine-tuning added persists where it no longer holds. SFT can thus appear to fine-tune the model successfully while silently teaching it to rely on spurious correlations rather than the video, leaving it vulnerable to any departure from its training distribution and diluting what makes it VideoLLM. Filtering the data before fine-tuning does not prevent the shortcut, and the rise in accuracy hides it afterward, so the intervention must come during fine-tuning, where the model can be made to ground its answer in the full input rather than the shortcut alone. This motivates our method, Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which keeps the fine-tuning update out of the directions where the text alone is read. VETO first calibrates the subspace carrying the shortcut from the activations produced by the text-only input at every layer, once per backbone. It then projects the LoRA update onto the orthogonal complement of that subspace during fine-tuning, so that the update cannot enter the directions in which the shortcut would be learned. As VETO constrains only the update, it leaves the prior the base model already carries untouched and allows the model to adapt to the video rather than to the shortcut. We evaluate VETO on the training distribution across seven VideoLLMs from five language models and on six unseen benchmarks. On the training distribution, VETO reaches nearly the same gain as SFT on every backbone, while the rise in text-only accuracy under SFT is largely suppressed. Under the shift VETO gains more over the base model than SFT, as Fig. 1(b) illustrates, and its reliance on the text rises far less than under SFT. VETO requires no definition of which regularity counts as the shortcut, no change to the data, loss, or schedule, and no cost beyond projection per step. Across experiments, the shortcut emerges not as an inevitable prior that fine-tuning must keep for its gain but as what stands between VideoLLM and the video it is given.

sections.title: 2 SHORTCUT FORMATION UNDER FINE-TUNING
sections.content: In this section we ask how the reliance of VideoLLM on the text changes over fine-tuning under the standard recipe for adapting it to target video QA task, SFT with LoRA (Hu et al., 2021). The base model is Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) and the target dataset is Something-Something v2 (SSv2) (Goyal et al., 2017a), whose answers come from fixed set of action templates. Under distribution shift we evaluate on Perception Test (Patraucean et al., 2023), whose videos, questions, and options differ from SSv2 and whose options are written freely rather than from templates.

sections.title: 2.1 BLIND FILTERING AND THE SHORTCUT
sections.content: Dataset preparation starts from the action template SSv2 assigns to every clip. We group the templates into families, where the templates of family share the same objects and scene and differ only in what happens over time. Examples are direction (moving left vs. moving right) and state transition (covering vs. uncovering X). The templates of family are thus hard negatives of one another, and no other template can serve as one. Each clip becomes one item, multiple-choice question in which the template of the clip is the correct option and the distractors are other templates rendered with the objects of the clip, with the families listed in Appx. A. Blind filtering removes the items that the base model already answers from the text alone. The full input pairs the video with the question and options, and the text-only input is the full input without the video. We query the base model three times per item under the text-only input with the option order shuffled each time and remove the item when it answers correctly in all three, so that lucky guess does not count. The filter applies to the training and evaluation splits alike, and on the evaluation split the base model reaches 19.3% text-only accuracy, below chance, as Appx. details. The shortcut is therefore any rise in text-only accuracy over fine-tuning, route to the answer that runs through the text alone and bypasses the video. Figure 2: The shortcut forms regardless of training epoch and data size. (a) The shortcut is present from the first epoch and persists. (b) The shortcut is substantial at every training set size, already at 1k items. Mean over three seeds. Figure 3: The shortcut forms regardless of backbone. Every VideoLLM gains large text-only accuracy after SFT.

sections.title: 2.2 BLIND FILTERING DOES NOT PREVENT SHORTCUT FORMATION
sections.content: Blind filtering removes every training item that the base model solves from the text alone, so SFT would seem to have nothing to learn from the text. Yet as Fig. 2(a) shows, the text-only accuracy rises together with the accuracy on the full input over the course of SFT, and the model ends up solving substantial fraction of the evaluation set without the video. SFT thus builds route through the text that the base model does not have. The shortcut forms regardless of training epoch. Fig. 2(a) tracks text-only accuracy over epochs, and it is far above chance from the first epoch. The shortcut is thus not overfitting late in training but part of what SFT learns from the start, and early stopping cannot avoid it. The shortcut forms regardless of data size. Fig. 2(b) plots the text-only accuracy against the training set size from 1k to all 57k items, and it is far above chance already at 1k and grows with the data as the accuracy does. The shortcut is thus not the noise of small sample that more data would average out, but regularity of the distribution that any sample of it carries. The shortcut forms regardless of backbone. Fig. 3 gives the text-only gain for seven VideoLLMs from five language models and sizes up to 32B, and each answers at least fifth more of the evaluation set from the text alone than its base model does. The shortcut is thus not particular to one language model or scale but what SFT does with the data.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: These three observations suggest that what the shortcut rests on is present regardless of the training schedule, the data scale, or the backbone. Blind filtering leaves only the items that the base model does not solve from the text alone, but that does not mean their text carries no information about the answer. The options each item receives in the dataset preparation are distinct sentences, and any regularity between their wording and the correct answer is there for SFT to pick up even where the base model does not read it. The regularity thus persists in the data under every variation, and it becomes the shortcut once SFT learns to read it.

sections.title: 2.3 WHY THE SHORTCUT MATTERS
sections.content: The purpose of SFT is to fit the target distribution for downstream tasks, and when that distribution carries regularity between the question and the answers, learning it can form shortcut. From Bayesian perspective this may not be defect. model that estimates prior from training data and combines it with the visual evidence at inference does what the objective asks, and rise in accuracy is consistent with that. Whether the shortcut is problem therefore turns on two properties of what has been learned: what the shortcut reads and whether the visual evidence still enters the decision. Table 1: Accuracy with the full input and from the text alone, on SSv2 and Perception Test. What the shortcut reads decides where it remains valid. The language prior the base model already carries reflects which actions tend to occur with which objects, and it holds where those facts hold. The shortcut is instead regularity of the training set, and such regularity may not hold once the questions and options are written differently. Tab. 1 tests this prediction on Perception Test, our evaluation set under shift, filtered as SSv2 is. On SSv2 the gap between the accuracy with the video and the accuracy from the text alone widens after fine-tuning, so the model gains more from the video than before and the shortcut sits alongside the reading of the video rather than replacing it. On Perception Test the same model reaches the accuracy of the base model it is fine-tuned from, while its accuracy from the text alone rises by 17.0 points, so the gap narrows and the shortcut has displaced much of what it drew from the video. What fine-tuning adds still raises the text-only accuracy on format it was never trained on, yet there it replaces part of the video reading and adds nothing to accuracy. The shortcut is therefore problem rather than prior the model needs. What it reads holds only within the training distribution, and under the shift it displaces the visual evidence instead of adding to it. The remaining question is where to intervene. Curating them further would require naming the regularity, which Sec. 2.2 does not. Once training ends, the shortcut is hard to detect, which leaves little room for remedy before or after training. Intervening on the training schedule is no easier, since the shortcut is in place regardless of epoch, data size, or backbone. What remains is training itself, and constraint at that stage would not teach the model more than fine-tuning already does, but it can suppress the shortcut as it forms.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: Fine-tuning baseline is standard SFT with rank-16 LoRA on the 57k items of the blind-filtered SSv2 training set of Sec. 2.1, with 16 frames per video, for up to 10 epochs at learning rate 104. We select checkpoints from held-out subset of the evaluation split that no reported accuracy uses, the same for every run. VETO trains under the identical recipe with the projection of Sec. 3.2 at ρ = 0.95. Every run uses single NVIDIA B200 GPU, and Appx. lists the remaining hyperparameters, the baseline implementations, and the seed statistics. Backbones span seven VideoLLMs from five language models, Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b) at 3B, 7B, and 32B, Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025a), LLaVA-OneVision-7B (Li et al., 2025), Molmo2-O-7B (Clark et al., 2026), and Gemma4-E2B (Team et al., 2026), each fine-tuned with the recipe above and calibrated against its own activations. Evaluation covers the SSv2 evaluation split and six benchmarks the fine-tuning never sees, Perception Test (Patraucean et al., 2023), Vinoground (Zhang et al., 2024), AoTBench (Xue et al., 2025), MVBench (Li et al., 2024), TVBench (Cores et al., 2024), and TempCompass (Liu et al., 2024). We blind-filter each set as in Sec. 2.1, and accuracy uses the highest-logit option letter as the answer. Appx. gives the counts.

sections.title: 4.3 SHORTCUT UNDER DISTRIBUTION SHIFT
sections.content: Tab. 2 reports the accuracy on Perception Test, whose videos, questions, and options all differ from SSv2. SFT raises text-only accuracy by 17.0 points overall and more than VETO in every area, so the shortcut of SFT carries over to this benchmark. On the full input, however, SFT is no better than the base model, whereas VETO improves over the base model while raising text-only accuracy much less. On this benchmark SFT keeps the shortcut but loses its gain, while VETO suppresses the shortcut and keeps its gain. Tab. 3 extends the comparison to five further unseen benchmarks, and VETO exceeds SFT on every one of them. VETO also brings far less of the shortcut into every benchmark than SFT, so the suppression carries over as well. Suppressing the shortcut is thus what makes the VideoLLM gain more than SFT under the shift.

sections.title: 4.4 WHERE THE VIDEOLLM GROUNDS ITS REASONING
sections.content: As VETO suppresses the shortcut while largely preserving the accuracy of the VideoLLM, pathway other than the shortcut has to carry that accuracy. This leads us to investigate where the VideoLLM grounds its reasoning on Qwen2.5-VL-7B throughout this section. To this end, we compare SFT and VETO on the full input and the text alone using two probes. The first probe asks where fine-tuning changes the computation on text. Under the text-only input we measure how far fine-tuning has moved the representation at each layer. The measure is the norm of the difference between the hidden states of the last token in the fine-tuned and the base model, relative to the norm in the base model. As presented in Fig. 6, SFT moves the representation further with depth, so the change that fine-tuning makes to the computation on text accumulates over the layers. VETO keeps it close to the base model at every layer. The invariance of Eq. 4 thus carries through the network. 7 Figure 6: Relative deviation from the base model per layer, text-only input.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Shortcuts and language priors have drawn extensive analysis since vision-language models (VLMs) came to rest on LLMs. In the image domain VLMs answer from the question alone (Goyal et al., 2017b; Agrawal et al., 2018), and in video many questions are likewise answered from text alone (Yang et al., 2025). The video is read as what typically happens rather than what the clip shows (Buch et al., 2022; Lei et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Fine-tuning then adds what its data teach, as VLM reproduces what is frequent in its instruction data regardless of the visual input (Li et al., 2023; Chen & Li, 2026). Such an added regularity is the shortcut, as distinct from the prior of the base model, and it predicts the label while it may not hold under distribution shift (Geirhos et al., 2020; Dancette et al., 2021; Agrawal et al., 2018). Remedies remove the bias from the data (Chen et al., 2020; Shvetsova et al., 2025), down-weight it in the loss through question-only model (Cadene et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019; Niu et al., 2021) or text-only penalty against the base model (Chen & Li, 2026), or correct the trained model through preference optimization (Wang et al., 2024) or its decoding through contrastive decoding (Yang et al., 2025). Each first defines the shortcut as quantity and then removes or penalizes it, but shortcut outside the definition lies outside the remedy (Dancette et al., 2021). Unlike for images, remedies for video still concentrate on the data and decoding rather than on training itself (Yang et al., 2025). VETO instead constrains the update, keeping it out of the directions in which the shortcut would be learned without defining it, so that the shortcut is suppressed as it forms rather than defined and removed. Constraining the update of fine-tuning to subspace separates what model maintains from what it modifies. Continual learning keeps gradients in the null space of features from earlier tasks (Wang et al., 2021) and the adapter subspaces of successive tasks orthogonal (Wang et al., 2023) or interference-free (Liang & Li, 2024), and model editing projects an edit onto the null space of the keys of knowledge it preserves (Fang et al., 2025). The same projection has been applied to representations rather than to updates (Ravfogel et al., 2020; Belrose et al., 2023), including to remove text-like subspace from the visual tokens of VLM (Saini et al., 2026). In all of these the subspace is defined by what the model already has and specified for it. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) gives the constraint its natural object, since its update enters the weights as few new directions (Shuttleworth et al., 2025). VETO then defines the subspace by what fine-tuning would read from the text, so that the same projection prevents rather than preserves. VETO adds only projection per step and needs no definition of the shortcut, which turns constraint built to preserve into one that prevents.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: This paper addresses the shortcut SFT builds in VideoLLM from textual regularities of its training data. The shortcut forms across VideoLLMs, yet it is not what fine-tuning requires for its gain and even costs accuracy under distribution shift. VETO suppresses the shortcut as it forms, preserves the gain of fine-tuning on the training distribution, and gains more than SFT under shift. What VETO calibrates is not list of regularities but where the text alone is read, so the same projection can make model use all of its input in other modalities. More broadly, what fine-tuning adds to VideoLLM is set not only by its data but by the directions its update is allowed to enter, and constraining the update is means of intervention the data, the loss, and the trained model do not offer.

sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
sections.content: Our analysis of the shortcut rests on multiple-choice video QA, where text-only accuracy can be measured directly. VETO itself is not restricted to this format, but free-form answering has no direct measure of the shortcut yet and is left to future work. The projection of VETO is instantiated with LoRA, and its extension to other adapters on the input side of the update is further direction. The main experiments fine-tune on SSv2 alone, and the same suppression of the shortcut is observed when fine-tuning on two further datasets, as Appx. reports.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools for correcting grammar, formatting tables, and placing figures in the paper. We have not used generative AI tools for preprocessing the training data, which follows the template of each dataset, and all videos and question-answer prompts come from publicly available datasets, with datasets such as Perception Test used under their license for academic research. The formulas in the paper were written by the authors, and generative AI tools were used only to typeset them in LaTeX. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to search for prior work that may overlap with the proposed method, so as to identify if there are any existing works with the same idea. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We have checked that every referenced work in the paper is relevant to the point the authors make with it. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO) is training-time technique that constrains how pretrained VideoLLM is fine-tuned. It operates on existing models and leaves the prior of the base model untouched, so it inherits their capabilities and limitations, including the biases in their pretraining data, and does not correct them. VETO is not safety filter and does not certify that model reasons from the video. model fine-tuned with VETO should therefore not be taken as faithful to its visual input beyond what is measured. Our experiments rely on publicly available VideoLLMs and on public video datasets used under their licenses, and no new data involving human subjects were collected. This work is intended for academic research. Any application of methods that shape what model learns during fine-tuning should document the calibration data and constraints used and follow the model and dataset licenses.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We will make the source code for VETO publicly available, including the calibration, projection, blind filtering, training, and evaluation pipelines together with the data manifests that define every split. The appendix provides the implementation details, including the fine-tuning recipe and hyperparameters, the construction of the calibration set and of the evaluation splits, and the pretrained models and datasets used in our evaluation, and every reported value is mean over the number of seeds stated there.

sections.content: A SSV2 FAMILY CONSTRUCTION Of the 174 SSv2 action templates (Goyal et al., 2017a), 47 come in hard-negative families of two to four templates. The templates of family share the same object placeholders and, once rendered for given clip, differ only in temporal content. We use these 47 in 16 families. Families fall into three tiers by the kind of temporal evidence they require. Direction families (horizontal, vertical, relative, two camera-motion families, object-relative) require the direction of motion. State-transition families (containment, cover, open-close) require the order of two states. Outcome families (lift, fall, spin, slant, poke, push, plug) require the result of an action that is visible only at the end of the clip. Each clip yields one multiple-choice question. The correct option is the template of the clip, and the distractors are the sibling templates re-rendered with the placeholders of that clip. For the eight two-template families we pad to four options with designated near-family distractors, which serve as options and never as answer sources, and the three-template family keeps its three options. sections.title: B BLIND FILTERING DETAILS
sections.content: We run the base model on each split under the text-only input three times with the option order shuffled, and discard items it answers correctly in all three. The rule keeps an item whenever the base model fails at least once in three, and the base model answers 19.3% of the kept items from the text, below chance. The filter removes 10.4% of the training pool, 63,526 to 56,922, and 10.7% of the evaluation pool, 8,977 to 8,016. sections.title: D IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Data splits follow Sec. 2.1. The blind-filtered SSv2 training set holds 56,922 items, of which 400 are drawn by stratified sampling over the families as the calibration set and held out, leaving 56,522 for training. The blind-filtered evaluation split holds 8,016 items, of which 200 drawn at random serve to select the checkpoint and the remaining 7,816 are the test set on which every accuracy of Sec. 4 is reported. The calibration, training, selection, and test sets are therefore pairwise disjoint. Backbones of Sec. 4.1, Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al., 2025b), Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025a), LLaVAOneVision (Li et al., 2025), Molmo2 (Clark et al., 2026), and Gemma 4 (Team et al., 2026), are listed in Tab. with their language model family and size, and with the accuracy of the base model on the SSv2 evaluation split with the full input and the text-only input. Training uses LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2021) on the attention and MLP projections of every decoder layer, with the down projection left untouched, and Tab. lists the settings. We optimize with AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) under cosine schedule for up to 10 epochs with early stopping on the selection accuracy, where the Qwen2.5-VL-7B runs of SFT and VETO complete all 10 epochs for the epoch curve of Fig. 2(a), with the checkpoint selected as in every other run. Attention uses FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) where the backbone supports it. Qwen2.5-VL-7B is trained with three seeds and reported as mean and standard deviation, the other backbones use the same three seeds, and Tab. gives the seed count of every row of Tab. 5 and Tab. 6. SFT and VETO share all of the above, and VETO adds only the projection of Sec. 3.2 after every optimizer step.
